source_text: Gratia vero Domini Iesu Christi non est ita data, ut per singula peccata, quasi per singula vulnera, singula quoque indulgentiae remedia provideret diversisque baptismatibus peccatis variis veniam praeberet, sed pro efficacissimae potestate medicinae, quae criminibus id est malae voluntatis operibus admovetur, ita communiter subvenit, ut diversas species reatuum unius vi consecrationis abstergat.
pass_a_gloss: But the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ was not so given, that through single sins, as through single wounds, it would also provide single remedies of indulgence and by diverse baptisms would offer pardon to varied sins, but according to the power of a most effective medicine, which is applied to crimes, that is to the works of an evil will, it so commonly comes to help that it wipes away diverse species of reatus by the force of one consecration.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'
LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, however, was not given so as to provide separate remedies of forgiveness for separate sins, as for separate wounds, and to pardon different sins through different baptisms. Rather, by the power of its supremely effective medicine, applied to crimes—that is, the works of an evil will—it gives comprehensive help, wiping away different kinds of guilt by the power of a single consecration.

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
